definition: Democratization means the process of making something accessible, inclusive, or available to ordinary people rather than a privileged few.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word democratization. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know democratization should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Cheap paperback printing drove the democratization of reading in the nineteenth century, putting books in the hands of workers who could never have afforded leather-bound volumes.
Outreach invites more people to try something, while democratization actually removes the barriers that kept ordinary people out.
Democratization makes something broadly accessible, and universalization goes even further, putting it within reach of absolutely everyone.

Popularization spreads something's fame or appeal, so far more people know it and want it. Democratization works on access instead: it removes the barriers of cost, privilege, or gatekeeping that kept ordinary people from actually having the thing. A pastime can be popularized yet stay too expensive for most; democratization is what finally opens the door.

Mainstreaming brings something into common, everyday use until it no longer seems niche or unusual. Democratization is about who can get it at all: opening access to ordinary people rather than a privileged few. A gadget can be mainstream among the well-off while its democratization — access for everyone else — has not yet happened.

For most of history, advanced math lectures were locked inside a handful of universities.
When free video courses appeared online, a farmer's daughter in a remote village could suddenly study the same material as students at elite schools.
Teachers uploaded problem sets, learners formed study groups across continents, and expertise stopped being a privilege of geography.
Educators hailed this democratization of learning as one of the internet's great gifts.
Advanced education became accessible to ordinary people everywhere instead of remaining a privilege of a select few, which is what democratization describes.

For decades, the city's woodworking scene belonged to those who could afford a garage full of equipment.
A decent table saw alone cost a month's rent.
Then the library system opened a tool-lending branch.
A library card -- free to any resident -- now checked out saws, sanders, and routers like novels.
Staff called the project the democratization of making: the barrier had never been interest or talent, only the price of entry.
Within two years, renters and teenagers were building furniture that once only homeowners with workshops could attempt.
The tools had not changed, a librarian pointed out.
What changed was who could get their hands on them.
